utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Zganjer, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before I begin that announce that I was going through my questions last afternoon and I could be finished within the first session, so until the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Zganjer, once again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can all the extra microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The topic we're going to discuss this morning is the Official Note. We've already discussed this at great length, but I should like to clarify certain issues and I would like to have your assistance in that. It is true, is it not, that the Official Note is, in fact, a form, a template that a police officer uses to record a pre-investigation action, be it an interview with a suspect or a witness, or a search of an area, a location, and so on and so forth? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, though I do want to correct you in one matter. It's not searching of an area, but going through an area inspecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the way in which the Official Note is made and the format used, it does not carry as much significance as other documents, such as the record of an interview with a witness or a scene of crime investigation report and so on. That is right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Official Note is only a piece of information and not a piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've just used the term information or notification. Notification for whom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the state attorney, who, before deciding to initiate criminal proceedings against a person, will draw upon the notification to learn certain facts that will be material to him to decide whether to initiate criminal proceedings against a person for a certain crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In essence, therefore, the Official Note represents an incentive for the judicial bodies, be it the state attorney or the investigating judge, to go through with the formal evidence and pursue investigation activities based on the information contained therein. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As for the Official Note made by the police once they've conducted interviews, it could be divided roughly into two segments: The Official Note of the interview conducted with a potential witness; and the Official Note of the interview with a suspect or a potential accused. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From a formal point of view, the procedural fate of such an Official Note is also a different one, when we talk about the two different types. So the Official Note of an interview held with a potential suspect must be, under the Croatian legislation, physically removed from the case file. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. It has to be removed, enveloped, and cannot be used in the presentation of evidence at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Exceptionally, though, it can be used where the accused specifically invokes that possibility. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I believe that the investigation judge or the trial judge hearing the case should, nevertheless, insist that the party concerned make the same statement before him as had been done before the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zganjer, in the course of your interviews with OTP investigators, you touched at great length also the topic of the Official Note, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was discussed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The OTP investigator, Mr. Robert Casey, in the course of the interview you had on the 12th of July, 2006, I'm referring to pages 16188 to 16189, practically put to you his view, his interpretation of the Official Note that -- notes that the police made at your request on the events in Grubori from the conversations with members of the special police and other individuals. He characterized them in the following way: That the interviews conducted were very poor, that they were not compiled in any sort of format, that the contents of these interviews did not really make a contribution or bring anything in, and that you should not perceive this as criticism levelled against you. Do you recall the investigator saying something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Casey did make certain comments, and Ms. Dave Morris I believe did so as well. She was present during my interview. But these were comments coming from the OTP, and I would not wish to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At any rate, some criticism was directed at you since a lot of time had elapsed between March 2002 and November 2002, when you received the information. However, you said that the incident at Grubori took place on the 25th of August, 1995, and that the police could have done something before 2001 as well. That was your position, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We broached the topic of the incident in the Grubori hamlet in the Plavno valley. You told us that at the time these events transpired, that's to say, the 25th of August, 1995, the body which had territorial and subject matter jurisdiction was the court in Zadar and, as a consequence, the state attorney's office in Zadar as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were informed of the case, once the jurisdiction was transferred, you initiated the procedure on your own initiative in order to establish what had actually transpired there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under the Croatian legislation, the state attorney has the power of initiating proceedings, and where there is no criminal report filed but the state attorney learns that something happened which might come under his jurisdiction. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian provisions, legal provisions regulating the work of the state attorney, state that the state attorney may become active on a case as soon as he receives reports or information of a criminal offence committed; in other words, there is no need for a criminal report to come from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, it is true, is it not, that in the majority of cases, that is the way in which proceedings are initiated by the state attorney; that's to say, a report or notification, whether it come from the police, from various inspection bodies, or from private citizens?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly, these are the most often ways in which the state attorney is prompted into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To put it colloquially, once you got into the case itself, once you were familiar well it, is it true - and I tell you what happened - you came to know that the Zadar state attorney's office had never received a criminal report concerning the events in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I learned. Not only that a criminal report had not been filed, but not even a regular report accounting the events in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to Exhibit P1061 on this issue, Your Honours. This is a letter, the correspondence between the state attorneys of Sibenik and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Zganjer, you came to know that once the incident in Grubori was entered into the log-book of the Knin police station, the general duty police did not dispatch a patrol in order to secure the crime scene. We discussed yesterday the fact that this should have been normally the first step taken in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just correct the record, this is a minor point; however, Mr. Mikulicic referred to P1061 as correspondence between the state attorneys of Zadar and Sibenik. It's actually correspondence between the state attorney of Zadar and the public prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zganjer, did you know Ive Kardum. Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We heard the testimony of Mr. Kardum, who, at the time of the events in Grubori, was the chief of the crime police in Zadar and who said that he had not been informed of the incident. However, what you have most certainly established is that no sort of a crime scene investigation was conducted in Grubori, either by the state attorney, investigating judge, or the police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, no follow-up forensic examination of the injuries sustained by the victims in order to ascertain the mechanism of injury in which the injuries were inflicted -- by which the injuries were inflicted, or the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Equally so, no evidence was collected from the crime scene. We see from your file that you asked the police to try and obtain the bullet casings you saw on the photographs and which had presumably been taken by the UN -- by the UN members. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, you were prompted by your report from Amnesty International to launch the proceedings. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was the first notification that I received about this incident, and it came from the Amnesty International staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that report, it is noted that one of the victims of the incident, Jovo Grubor, had been killed in such a way that he was slaughtered, that his throat was slit. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Amnesty International report did mention the fact that one of the persons, Jovo Grubor, or perhaps somebody else, had simply had his throat cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the course of the proceedings in which you tried to establish facts, was this fact really established by an expert through an examination of the body or perhaps an autopsy performed by a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the case was in my hands, I don't think that we were ever able to establish this fact, so this remained a claim that was made in the Amnesty International report. It never went beyond this claim, but I do allow that it was possible when the victims were exhumed from the Knin cemetery that the body of Jovo Grubor was among those exhumed. I attended the exhumation, but in the mean time, I had left Sibenik. I do know for a fact that the report on this exhumation and the autopsies or post-mortem examinations that followed later was submitted to the state attorney's office. Now whether Jovo Grubor's body really was exhumed in that exercise, I cannot claim that with full certainty, but I do allow that this was possible; and if, indeed, it was exhumed, I don't know what was ascertained upon the examination of Jovo Grubor's body. I would not now like to bother the Court with details, but if we're talking about any evidence of his throat being cut, it is possible that no evidence was actually found because of the decomposition. That is a consequence of the body being buried for such a long time. This is just a layperson's assessment, so that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question, do you remember -- regarding the incident that occurred in August 1995, as we said, do you remember when the exhumation and the autopsy of the bodies were conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 2001. I think it was in 2001 in mid-April or May, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zganjer, let me go back to the interview that you had with the OTP investigators. The OTP investigator, Robert Casey, put it to you that there is no doubt there was an attempt to cover-up things; by that, he means the Grubori incident by the special police. Now, question to you is this: As examined the materials that were at your disposal that you were able to collect, did you ever obtain any evidence or any knowledge that this claim that the Prosecution put to was based on facts, facts that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the facts that I had at that time, I could not reach a conclusion that this was, indeed, an attempt to cover up. But I have to say that, as far as I'm concerned, it was inconceivable to me why this event was not reported to the duty investigating judge and the duty state attorney. This was an incident of such a nature and of such a scope that, simply, this incident should not have engendered any kind of academic debate, whether this should have been reported to the investigating judge and the state attorney, because it is without a shadow of a doubt, it's a case that should have been reported to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, do you know that special police members are not the element of the police force that carries out crime investigations -- crime scene investigation, and they are not the part of the police force that submits reports to the investigating judge and so on? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Special police has clearly defined special tasks, interviewing, citizens or suspects, conducting crime scene investigations, taking other operational crime investigation measures. These are not the tasks of the special police; that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, you said that the mere fact that the state attorney received word or a report of a crime, this is enough to prompt them into action. As you conducted actions on the Grubori case, did you come across any facts that indicated that there was an attempt to cover up or to in any other way tamper with the investigation from any side. In that case, you would have to institute criminal proceedings against any such party?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite naturally. In such a situation, I would have tried to clarify all the circumstances in which this attempt to tamper or cover up of this whole incident by those persons was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic: As you dealt with the Grubori case while you were the state attorney in Sibenik, did you ever obtain any evidence or learn anything to the effect that General Markac did anything to, in effect, prevent any investigation into the Grubori incident and clarification of the circumstances of the incident? Did you come across any traces of this activity on part of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the materials that I had at my disposal, I was unable to establish any facts that would indicate that I should reach such a conclusion, the conclusion that Mr. Markac had in any way prevented or obstructed the actions of the police regarding the Grubori incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document P505, MFI, could I please have this document on the screen; P505, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, you will see this document in front of you. It's a document that you received from the police, and it's a document, it's a purported memorandum from the special advisor to the minister of the interior, Mr. Mladen Markac, to the minister of the interior, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak. In response to the Prosecution questions, you said that you had no reason to doubt the authenticity and credibility of this document because, at your request, it was submitted to you by the competent authorities, the Ministry of Interior in this case. I fully respect and understand your position, and, honestly, I would have the same position in the circumstances because I did the same job as you did for a number of years. However, because of certain circumstances, in particular, pertaining to this issue, I have come to suspect the authenticity and credibility of this document, and let me now draw your attention to some of the defects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you're introducing, first of all, your personal experience, what your feelings were. Of course, we are here to hear the testimony of the witness, rather than your --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... my testimony, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- testimony. And if you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I was trying to put my case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there's no problem with leading, but at a certain moment, it becomes counterproductive. Could you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to avoid this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zganjer, could you please look at the heading or the letterhead in this document and, in particular, the number which begins -- the reference number which begins with 511-01-30, and now this is an empty space here. It is usual practice - could you please confirm that or not - that usually the number from the registry book is entered here and the first figures listed here define the body, designate the body that actually issued this document, and it is quite clear that the numbers that are put in by the registry book are missing here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we now go back to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the registrar to move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We can see that Mladen Markac is designated here as the person issuing the document, but the document is unsigned and there is no official stamp on this document. It is usual for documents, official documents, to bear both. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I confirm that. It is quite usual that such documents are signed by the drafter and an official stamp is affixed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In light of those circumstances, I went one step further and I sought official information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D01-0565 up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will have it in front of us. However, I sent a letter to the office for the Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal with the Ministry of Justice, and I asked them to let me know, under item 1, whether the controversial document, if it exists, was, in fact, signed. I asked for a signed copy of this document to be sent to me. I also wanted them to let me know whether the registry book of the special police sector, for the year 1996, if there is any trace that would indicate that this document signed by General Markac was, in fact, sent and received in the office of the then-minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, and, furthermore, whether any such document was later on forwarded to the Special Rapporteur, Elisabeth Rehn, from Mr. Jarnjak's office? Mr. Zganjer, you can see this in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D909 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received an answer to this letter or request, and that is document 3D01-0563.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I received this reply from the Directorate for International Cooperation of the Justice Ministry. It was signed and stamped by Mr. Markotic who is the head of the directorate, and we can see here that all the registry numbers are in place. I am notified in this letter that from the Justice Ministry -- or rather, from the Ministry of Interior, they received information that they have checked in their archives and were unable to find a signed copy of the document at issue. Furthermore, this memo was not entered in the registry book for the relevant time-period; that is, 1996, of the former assistant minister for special police, General Markac, and a copy of his personnel file is provided by the directorate. In the last paragraph, they note that the file was not entered -- that this document was not entered in the registry books of the office of Minister Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D910, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D910 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the registry to show document 3D01-0567.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the registry book of the special police sector which at that time, in 1996, did exist. It's a huge book, of course, and we will now look at the entries for the dates in question, and that's the 13th of March, 1996, and this is the date listed on the controversial document as the date that the document was actually issued. We can see in the upper area that this page starts with the date which is the 12th of March; and then further down the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I am asking myself what exercise we are engaged in at this moment. The witness gave his view on face value of a document, and it's clear from that what the basis of his assessment is. The basis would not easily allow for any inferences as to whether that is correct or not. He just gives his impression, the impression he gains on the basis of that document. Now you're taking us through a lot of apparent verification exercises on the authenticity of this document. Now, what would we expect the witness then at then end to say, "Well, I was wrong, I was right." I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That would be my final questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, these are questions for the Court to decide --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether he was right or whether he was wrong. We are not asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That would not be my question whether he was right or he was wrong. My question would be, if he knew then those facts, would it be that his impression would be the same. That would my final question, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a hypothetical question, if you would have had another knowledge, would you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah, like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a matter of logic, rather than anything else, isn't it? You think that the -- of course, if the witness could say, "Well, I know that these records or these registers are not complete; therefore, I would have to doubt to say so," et cetera. But, of course, I'm asking myself whether providing this information to the Chamber, and as argument to add to that, please keep sharply in mind that what the witness says is just based on his --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what he knew at the time. We, and especially you, Trial Chamber, you know far more about the matter. So if evaluating, at face value, the assessment of this witness, please keep in mind that the witness was not aware of that and that. Then I'm inclined to say that we could do the job, because the job is about -- simply, it is if you have an initial, a provisional assessment of a situation, if you add information, would that affect the assessment, if the witness would say no. Of course, if he can add anything to that, if you have any knowledge about this or to say that this is incomplete, or "I know for certain that these records have been checked, and I know that it was always established that there were complete." So if something is not in there, it could not -- I mean, if he has any such knowledge, I would certainly like to know for sure, because then he adds to what apparently is documentary evidence which gives a further insight in what this letter may be. Therefore, I'm asking whether this witness can add anything to what I take it, Ms. Mahindaratne, I heard of no objection, additional information, you accept as being obtained from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please keep that in mind, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure, Your Honour. If the witness just can answer my final question, whether he would state within his impression, it was impression because he said that the document came through the channels of the Ministry of Interior, and, therefore, he estimated his authenticity and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we can be very clear. Verification seems not to confirm, Mr. Zganjer, does not confirm that the letter was sent and/or received. If you would have had this information at the time, and since you see this kind of information now, would you find that a reason to reconsider your first impression of authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I was aware of that information at the time -- had I been aware of the information at that time, I would have called into question what I thought. What I see now drives me to believe that there was some kind of a game played within the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D911, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D911 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zganjer, at the time you worked and was -- were active in the Sibenik state attorney's office, you were faced with certain activities that the Ministry of Justice or the state attorney of the Republic of Croatia undertook in terms of seeking information about actions taken, statistics concerning crime, and so on and so forth. This could be called the usual activity, could it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the usual activity in which every state attorney's office engaged periodically, and regularly at the end of the year informing the Ministry of Interior of the number of received criminal reports, and informed the state attorney's office of the actions taken on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will show to you a document concerning the military judiciary, the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the registrar please call up 3D01-0561.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the memo from the then-minister of justice, Mr. Separovic, dated 5th of January, 1996, addressed to the presidents of the military courts in Zagreb, Bjelovar, Osijek, Karlovac, and Split, as can you see. In this memo, the ministry, in paragraph 2, seeks to be notified of the court proceedings against perpetrators of crimes committed after the military and police Operation Storm, regardless of whether the proceedings were pending against persons of Serb ethnicity or persons of Croat ethnicity, or members of the Croatian army. Mr. Zganjer, were you aware at that time of this practice whereby the Croatian authorities sought information on the criminal proceedings pending; thus, wishing to be informed about the number and type of criminal proceedings carried out after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you are showing to me here on the screen is a document sent to the presidents of military courts. I was not familiar with the specific document, since it had to deal with military courts. However, I knew that the Ministry of Justice, through the state attorney's office of the Republic of Croatia, sought, at the time, roughly the same sort of information from state attorney's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The competent state attorney was duty-bound to inform the chief state attorney of the information?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the district or county state attorney's offices collected various information which was then compiled at the level of the national state attorney's office and forwarded to the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, while you were performing the duty of a state attorney, did you personally ever receive any sort of instruction or order that in the course of criminal proceedings, you should make some concessions, refrain from certain criminal proceedings, or characterizations of certain crimes? Did you ever receive such sort of information from anyone in the various structures of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel Mikulicic, all my life throughout my career in the state attorney's office, I worked by following my conscience, and I was never asked by anyone to turn a blind eye to anything. I was primarily in the service of my conscience rather than the service. That would be my answer, rather than in the service of my position. I was never told by anyone to turn a blind eye or to not see things clearly on any matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from any of your colleagues that anybody else, be it in your state attorney's office or in other state attorney's offices that you were in contact with, had been subjected to such influence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the Sibenik state attorney's office and my deputies, they knew full well what my professional work ethic was, and nobody could have excerpted any sort of pressure upon them without me knowing about it. They were responsible for their jobs to me; and me, by virtue of my position being the state attorney, I protected them from the higher levels, be it the Ministry of Justice or the national state attorney office, regardless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Zganjer, on the issue of -- that we're discussing now. When you left the Sibenik office, you ceased working on the Grubori case. You said that at that time you left, the case was still open, it had not been closed. Do you have any information as to whether this same case is closed today or whether the investigation is still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I do not have any specific knowledge about that. In the month of September of 2002, I assumed a different position within the state attorney system, whereupon I left the state attorney's offices. I have to be frank, that due to the great workload that I had to take on after I left the Sibenik state attorney's office, I did not have time or interest to know what was going on. When I left the state attorney's offices system altogether in February 2006, I did not have any way of knowing what was going on in the Grubori case in operative terms; that's to say, after the 15th of February, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Equally so, I believe you have no knowledge as to whether the potential suspects or perpetrators of the Grubori incidents were identified.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't believe that they have been identified so far. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the screen into the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D912, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D912 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kay, or Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't know whether you were third in line or second in line without questions. Thank you. Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic, Mr. Zganjer, is counsel for Mr. Gotovina and he will now cross-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me start, Mr. Registrar, if can I call up 1D60-0074.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me start, Mr. Zganjer, with where you left off with Prosecutor yesterday, which is this issue of the admissions or confessions that had been made in the Varivode case, and you said that the confession was made in front of the investigating judge, which is correct. But I'd like to show you statement of one of the accused or the Official Note of the interview of one of the accused before he went to the investigating judge, which is the Official Note of the interview of the subsequently accused Zlatko Ladovic. The note was taken by Ivo Kardum. You will recognise that he was at the time the chief of the crime police in the Zadar-Knin police administration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the information on the screen, but I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we can go to page 2 in the English, which is also page 2 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ladovic talks about - it's quite long; it's a three-page Official Note - but he talks about the events in Varivode. If we start --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I won't go through the whole thing in order to save time. If we go to six lines below the line that has "Jakovljevic, Ivan" in bold - it's six lines in the English and I am not sure how many in Croatian - the sentence begins: "He says that Coro was wearing the camouflage pants ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now Mr. Ladovic, according to the Official Note, says: "He says that Coro was wears camouflage pants and a black shirt, that his hair was tied, and that he was carrying an automatic rifle. Zlatko and Zuki moved forward, and Coro and the short, blond guy stayed behind them. He states how he move -- sorry. He states how he asked Zuki where the Chetniks were and that he responded ahead. Coro and the blond guy headed towards a garden and that he and Zuki continued along the road." Then a few lines below that, he talks about Ivica Petric, and then he says: "He states that at one point, unexpectedly, Zuki fired at these civilians from an automatic rifle, and he didn't know what to do, until he realized what was going on. Seeing what Zuki did them, he said to him, 'Zuki, those aren't Chetniks. What are you doing?' Then he replied, 'It doesn't matter, this is the same gang.'" Then it goes on to details about the killing of other civilians as well in Varivode. Now, my question goes back to these Official Notes. You ultimately decided that the confession before the investigating judge, as well as the confession made at least in the Official Note to Mr. Kardum, did not even provide a reasonable basis to proceed with the Varivode indictments. My question for you is: What is it about this Official Note that was not credible to you as a basis for proceeding with charges against Mr. Ladovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to explain a couple of things to you. The Official Note that Counsel Misetic has shown me was not of interest to me when I received this case for my action. When I received this case for my action - that was in 1999, if I'm not mistaken - I focussed in particular -- or rather, I only focussed on the confessions made by some of the accused before an investigating judge, and this is what I really have to stress: Before an investigating judge. These people - Ladovic - were questioned by a investigative judge. And in this stage, when the Supreme Court quashed the judgement and ordered a retrial, I only took into account Ladovic's statement and Jakovljevic's statement made before the investigating judge because only those statements were used as evidence at trial, and I could only evaluate them, not an Official Note. This is why I see no need for any reference to be made to this Official Note. There is the -- there are statements of four of the accused in this case, given to an investigative judge; and this is an Official Note that we discussed at length in the proceedings. This is merely a notification; it is not evidence. In this case, as regards the statement by Ladovic, as a citizen, or as a suspect, we had his statement given to an investigating judge; and when the case came to me, I focussed on analysing the parts of the case file that had evidentiary value. This Official Note does not have evidentiary value; whereas, Zlatko Ladovic's statement before an investigating judge does have such value. This is why I focussed on that statement, not on this Official Note, because I could not come to court and tell the judge, "I'm sorry, judge, but this what is he said in his Official Note," because the Court would simply brush aside this intervention, and they would say, "Now you're referring to something that is not contained in the case file," because this Official Note had been redacted from the case file a long time ago as material that cannot be used as evidence in criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up. You were asked some questions -- and, first, let me just explain to you, Mr. Zganjer, what we're trying to do here, first, with these Official Notes is determine their reliability. You were asked some questions on this point both by the Prosecutor and by the Presiding Judge yesterday. What I'd like you to do -- even though you did not have this in the case file, you are aware of the facts of the case against Mr. Ladovic because you ultimately decided not to prosecute him. So what I'd like you to explain to us is, now looking at the Official Note and Mr. Ladovic's acknowledgment, at least in the Official Note, of the events in Varivode and his presence there, my question is: Looking at this, do you consider this a reliable statement to the police; and, if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this statement by Mr. Ladovic, this Official Note of an interview with Mr. Ladovic, was, at any rate, a useful piece of information. But useful for whom? The county state attorney's office in Zadar at the time when the criminal report against the four people was received. At that time, this Official Note became a relevant document for them, enabling them to decide whether criminal proceedings should be launched against those persons or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand the procedural issues that you're addressing. Let me phrase the question a different way. The official police note says that Mr. Ladovic says he was in Varivode with Zuki and Ivica Petric, and Coro and Zuki fired at civilians in Varivode and killed civilians in Varivode. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. I think this witness cannot answer that question as to whether that is true or not. He has explained what the notes are and their purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. The objection is granted. But I do see what you'd like to know, Mr. Misetic. This Official Note first reflects a statement given to police officers by Mr. Ladovic. Do you have any reason to believe that the Official Note does not accurately reflect what Mr. Ladovic told the police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do allow that what the police officer recorded when interviewing the citizen or suspect Ladovic is, indeed, accurate. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is an answer to my first question. If you'd like to add anything at a later stage, you may do so. If you would, please, listen to my second question: Do you have any reason to believe that what was put on paper as the statement or what was put on paper as reflecting what Mr. Ladovic had told the police officers was not in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I have to admit that I cannot recall details from Mr. Ladovic's statement, the statement that he gave to the police officers. I do allow that this is what he really did say to the police officers, and that they recorded this accurately in the Official Note. However, Mr. Ladovic spoke about this in his interview with the investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I would kindly ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say the reasons for believing or the reasons to doubt the truthfulness of his statement is found in the later statement he gave to the investigating judge, if you say on the basis of what I've seen there, I have doubts as to whether he told us the truth - not us, of course - he told the truth to the police officers, if that is what you want to draw our attention to, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for this intervention. You, in fact, may have rendered in the most accurate terms what I have been trying to say. I have reason to doubt the contents of the statement because what he said to the police, and in particular what he said to the investigating judge, he and the other accused, well, what they told the investigating judge in particular has nothing to do with the scene of the crime. It is enough for you to look at what they said in the course of the investigation and to look at the photo file where the crime scene is recorded. You can see that it simply cannot be true. The manner in which they described having killed some people does not correspond to what was established at the crime scene, and you don't have to be a genius. All you have to is read in detail their confessions and look at the photographs, and you can see that there is something wrong with the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I do understand you well, you say that the reasons for you to believe if the Official Note accurately reflects what he said, the reason is that the statement he gave to the investigating judge is not consistent with what he apparently told the police. You add to that that the details he gave do not match the information you had available on the events. I, when trying to understand your testimony, I noticed myself - I might be mistaken, where I said inconsistent - I haven't seen that material. But I'm trying to understand what you're telling us. You say: This is apparently what he told, he gave a statement at a later stage to the investigating judge, and details he describes there do not match with the information he had about the events, the terrain, and the circumstances. Have I understood your answer well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, that's what I'm trying to say. If you allow just one more remark, as far as I can recall, after seven or eight years, one of the accused said more or less the following: We were moving down the road towards the village of Varivode; and at one point, two people we didn't know in uniform came towards us, and I automatically turned my machine-gun towards them and shot them, killing them. None of the victims were found on the road. The event that one of the accused described would indicate that there was a certain distance between those people and him, the man who fired the shots. The people in Varivode were killed in their own yards. They were killed as they sat at their tables, in front of their homes. For the most part, they were shot in the head. They were shot in the head in their own front yards. This is what I can recall. So this confession, this story about how those two people were killed, the circumstances as they with described, has nothing to do about what was established on the crime scene. I'm sure that you have the files, that you have the photo file, and it would a very simple exercise to look at that time and come to this conclusion, to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, my question on this topic, in light of your answers, is this: In light of your 27 or 28 years of experience in the Croatian criminal justice system, do you have any insight that you could offer us as to why these defendants, and in this particular case, Mr. Ladovic, would tell the police or confess to the police that he, in fact, had participated in the murders in Varivode?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know how the witness could respond to that question as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know whether he can answer. He is asked whether, in his experience, whether he could offer any reason, in this particular case, why they would have told the police that they were involved. We don't know. If he can't explain, he will tell us. If he has any information which would help him and help us to understand this confession, he'll tell us. Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my response, I can only refer to what, in the course of the proceedings, the accused actually did say, and what they did say is that they were beaten brutally by police officers. I cannot confirm that, but I cannot rule that out. I do know that had I been the state attorney at the time when they were brought into custody, I would have asked them to show me the evidence for this abuse that they allegedly suffered at the hand of the police officers, and then I would ask the investigating judge to record all this evidence. In that case, that would give more or less credence to what they were saying. But this is what they stated in the course of the investigative proceedings before a court in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1D60-0074 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D913.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D913 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now have P1062 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the special report that you were shown by the Prosecutor of the 27th of June, 2002, by Mr. Glavan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in the English of this report, please. And if we could scroll down please in the English, and it's page 2 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now the second paragraph from the bottom in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down in the English text please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "Furthermore, according to the information collected, Nenad Mrkota and other persons, together with Bozo Bacelic currently in detention of the county court in Sibenik, put pressure on the witnesses in the criminal procedure for the crime committed in Prukljani and crimes committed in Gosici and Varivode, suspected of being committed by Bozo Bacelic and Goran Vunic." Now, Mr. Zganjer, this is sent to you at the end of June in 2002, and I note from the Prukljani case, which you prosecuted, there was a trial six weeks later -- I'm sorry, ten weeks later in September of the same year, in which Goran -- in this case, it says Bozo Bacelic and Goran Vunic were together, suspected of committing the crimes in Gosici and Varivode; yet ten weeks later in the trial against Bacelic, one of the witness against him was Goran Vunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can see that in Exhibit D843, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Zganjer: After receiving this report, between the time you received this report and, ultimately, when Mr. Vunic testified against Mr. Bacelic ten weeks later, did you do anything to ask Mr. Vunic or question him or take any other measure to investigate any basis for the allegation that he was involved in the murders in Gosici and Varivode?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel Misetic, let me first clarify one thing. I received the document on or around the 27th of June, 2002. You're talking about some ten weeks after that. I don't know what ten weeks are we talking about. The judgement in the Bozo Bacelic et al case for the Prukljani case was made public on the 12th of September, 2002. It appears to me that if you're talking about Goran Vunic, that in the Prukljani case, Goran Vunic was examined as a witness before I received this document, that is, before the 27th of June, 2002; but, of course, we can check that by inspecting the case file. I do know for a fact that the judgement was made public in the Bozo Bacelic et al case on the 12th of September 2002. I also know for a fact that Goran Vunic was a witness that was called in that case, and I think that Goran Vunic was examined as a witness at this trial before I received this document that you're now showing me. Now we have to check the case file and see when Goran Vunic was actually examined as a witness in that case, in that trial. So if you can be more specific with your question. So I would like to ask you to take this caveat into account, and perhaps I could prompt you to verify what I have just told you in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will do that during the break, and then we'll continue this topic after the break, Mr. Zganjer. But while we're on this document, regardless of whether he -- the date of his testimony, you now have enough information at the end of June 2002 certainly that Mr. Mrkota participated in the crime of obstructing a criminal investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I received this notice, I had quite specific information about all this. There was the statement by Davor Simic, a police officer. As far as I can recall, there was his work plan, there were search warrants that were never actually implemented. So I did have information that for some reasons, Nenad Mrkota may have obstructed the police action, actions aimed at Goran Vunic. So it is true, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What happened? What was the result of your investigation of Mr. Mrkota's obstruction of the criminal investigation in Varivode?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said a few times, in September, I went to Zagreb. So now we're talking about late June. But if the Court is interested in this, I can tell you what doubts I had when it comes to Nenad Mrkota and the facts that transpired relating to his actions. So, here, we have notice or notification that Nenad Mrkota may have obstructed police actions; in other words, actions conducted by himself, because Davor Simic was in the company that was under the command of Mrkota. So how could we qualify this in operational terms, in legal terms? If it is, indeed, true that Nenad Mrkota knew in advance what Bozo Bacelic and Goran Vunic would do in Gosici, and if he promised that he would assist them in this manner by obstructing the police investigation, then, in that case, Nenad Mrkota would be held criminally responsible for aiding a murder or perhaps even a war crime, if he promised he would help them in advance knowing what they would do at a certain location. But if, in fact, Nenad Mrkota learned what Bozo Bacelic and Goran Vunic had purportedly done at a later stage, then his conduct could be qualified as aiding a perpetrator after the commission of the crime. So if we're talking about this crime, aiding after the fact, then at the time when we received this notification, seven years, almost full seven years after the crime was committed, we would be in an area where the statute of limitations had already expired in relative terms, and we could not prosecute Nenad Mrkota. And if the former was the case, if he knew in advance what they would do and if he promised to assist them, then there would be no statute of limitations. We were in a legal quandary here. We had to resolve that and take action as appropriate. Now, whether, after I left, the state attorney's office thought along those lines and conducted appropriate checks, I can't tell you. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just correct the record, the witness said Davor Simic, and it's been recorded as Davor Simir, but I think also the witness was referring to Damir Simic, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was on my mind as well. As you also know, usually the transcripts are reviewed after we leave the courtroom, and it is a lot of work, but it certainly will assist those who are hearing the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last question before the break, Mr. Zganjer: Did you ever consider at the time you received the report on the screen, that, in fact, the opposite was true and someone was obstructing the investigation in Varivode by claiming that Mr. Mrkota was, in fact, obstructing the investigation of the "real perpetrators"? In other words, did you ever consider that someone was trying to assist the accused -- the existing accused in the Varivode case by coming up with an alternative theory?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Varivode and Gosici cases, which were conducted against certain persons, we came by certain facts and information which led us to suspect that the crimes in Varivode and Gosici were committed by other individuals altogether, individuals wearing the uniform of the Croatian army, because the witnesses in that case made statements along those lines. You certainly must have the statements of these witnesses who said that before hearing the gun-fire from Gosici, they had seen trucks with uniformed individuals heading toward Gosici. After that, they heard gun-fire again and, upon arriving in the area, saw what they saw. That's what some witnesses said in no unclear terms, if I recall that well. Among others, this was one of the facts which led us to suspect that the possible perpetrators are either members of the Croatian army or persons who put on Croatian army uniforms ad hoc. There were quite a few of those, you know, at the time who would put on Croatian army uniforms in order to go and borrow things from abandoned homes. They wore the uniform of the Croatian army, but whether they were actually members of that army is a big question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... moment, Your Honour. This would be a good time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D843 on the screen, please. If we could go to page 2 in the Croatian and page 4 in the English version, please, and down at the bottom of the page in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I'm just showing you this so that maybe you can help us clarify this. In the actual judgement for the Prukljani murders in the Bacelic case, it says that the indictment was issued on the 1st of March, 2002 and amended on 1 March 2002, as well as on 23 August 2002 at the main hearing. That's where I came to the conclusion that the trial took place on 23 August 2002, but maybe you can clarify. Do you recall when and over how many days the trial in the Bacelic case took place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trial definitely started after the indictment was filed. If it says here that the indictment was filed on the 1st of March, 2002, then the trial must have ensued after that date. I can't recall at this time if the indictment was challenged in any way, but this does not change my statement that the trial must have started after the 1st of March 2002. It is also true that one of the hearings in that case was held on the 23rd of August, 2002. It is also true that the trial ended on the 11th of September, 2002, when this judgement was published, the one you're showing right now on the screen. I'm now correcting the part of my statement where I said that the judgement was published on the 12th of September. I think that I saw on the cover page of this judgement that it was published or rendered on the 11th of September, 2002, and I change that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I will move on to a different topic, and I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could call up 1D60-0001, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, what I'm going to you is the actually operative action plan that the MUP came up with on the 15th of October, 1995, as its a plan to establish the identity of the perpetrators of the homicides in the settlements of Varivode and Gosic. Now, this is the 15th of October, and you will note some of the names: Pero Perkovic; Zvonimir Lasan Zorobable; Zlatko Ladovoc, whose statement we've looked at this morning; Ivica Petric; Boris Vunic; Nedeljko Mijic; and on the right-hand side, Nikola Rasic Zes. The work plan states that by 0300 hours on the 16th, the correct addresses need to be established for these individuals. I ask you to note here that the only person so far with the last name of Vunic who is suspected by the MUP is Boris Vunic on the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not principally object to this document, but you can see page 3 and 4 of the documents are missing from the Croatian version as well as the English version. From what I can see, there is a signature at page 2; but at page 3, I don't know whether that is supposed to be an attachment or what it is. Page 3 is numbered as page 5, so obviously page 3 and 4 are is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will be happy to disclose that counsel. It is not a big deal to us. Actually, we added the page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, if you could turn to that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, it is the last page in this exhibit. Because in the attachment to the MUP plan, it says that the subject of the search is going to be the house of person Vunic Boris, son of Ante, born on 20 December, 1971. So, Your Honour, to satisfy Ms. Mahindaratne, I ask that the exhibit be MFI'd, and I will come up with pages 3 and 4 for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I agree to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D914, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to the work plan, interviews were conducted with some of the persons who are named in the wok plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D60-0007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, let me ask you a preliminary question. If, during the course of an interview or an investigation of one criminal event, the police and/or the prosecutor's office learns of the commission of a different crime, what is the obligation of the police and/or the prosecutor's office with respect to the additional crime uncovered in the investigation? In other words, do they have an obligation to investigate that additional crime as well?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there is such an obligation. The course of a criminal investigation is always unpredictable, one way or the other. You could be initiating the proceedings for one crime, and then you may come across helpful information indicating that other crimes may have been committed in addition to the one you were investigating. Generally speaking, the police uses such information in order to investigate these other lines, indicating the commission of other crimes. The police will inform the state attorney's office of that information. But, as a rule, the police will always do whatever can be done today, today, rather than leaving it for tomorrow. If there is indication that certain actions need to be taken right away in order to obtain useful information, the police will do so, with a view to getting the information necessary. Of course, the police will inform the state attorney of all the useful information they have gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me take to you this statement now, and this is where Mr. Lasan talks about, towards the middle of the page: "Upon entry to the house, Zvonimir told them he had killed the old man, but he cannot remember the exact words he used. After staying there for a short time, they left that village; and on their way to Kistanje, they met Petric and Patko who were also on their way to visit the area." Then it goes down, I believe, to the last sentence: "Aside from this murder, Zvonimir states that he didn't kill or shoot at anyone else after Operation Storm, besides shooting at some Chetniks during the operation and burning one house when they entered Kistanje, which he thought was a Chetnik house because he saw a lot of books there that were mostly in Cyrillic and a picture of a man in a Yugoslav uniform." Now, my question is: There seems to be specific information about at least one of the perpetrators of a burning houses in Kistanje. Do you know if anything was done on the basis of this information to prosecute this individual, or anyone else who was with him, for setting fires in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have specific information about that; however, I would like to draw everybody's attention to one fact. This statement taken by the police officer, from the citizen Zvonimir Lasan, was taken in 1995 in relation to the Varivode and Gosici events, if I'm not mistaken. This statement, in addition to the criminal report against certain individuals for the crimes committed in Varivode and Gosici, was given to the Zadar state attorney. The year was 1995, and the area of Kistanje is mentioned here, which also came under the Zadar-Knin police administration purview and the purview of the Zadar state attorney. Now, whether they, on the basis of the information provided by Citizen Zvonimir Lasan, acted in any way as a follow-up, that's something I don't know. I repeat: The proceedings were conducted by the Zadar-Knin police administration. A moment ago, you showed me the work plan that was drafted by the Sibenik police administration. Nothing strange there. What was involved was a serious crime and the stage was that of the pre-criminal proceed. In the attempt to identify the perpetrators of the crime, the members of the Zadar and Sibenik police administrations were involved; however, the case was so serious that the Zagreb crime police administration got involved as well, as did the military police, and the security an information service, too. The case was such that it demanded an all-encompassing police investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, principally I would not object, but this is a matter that I raised with Mr. Misetic last evening. We have only one paragraph, and there's another paragraph that has been translated. So, at this stage, I'm unable to, you know, make any sense of what the rest of the notice is. This is not a huge document, and I believe parties generally submit partial translation where the documents are large. But we're now talking about a record of interview from a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters simple. If you would be granted another 24 hours to review whether the remainder of the document would cause to you ask the Chamber to reconsider admission or to reconsider the extent to which this document should be admitted into evidence, as far as translation is concerned, would that that do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then we'll ask Mr. Registrar already to assign a number. We'll give a decision on admission, but you're in a position to revisit the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D915.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D915 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D60-0014 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a statement or an Official Note, I should say, of an interview with Berislav Setkanic, and I only put it on the screen because it was taken as part of the Varivode, Gosic investigation. It has a reference to Vunic Bore, which is short for Boris, with a description, and stating that he knows some of the individuals. Two of them are friends with Nikola Belic. But in any event, it is Boris Vunic who is referenced or whose name comes up in the course of the Varivode, Gosici investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection on the same basis, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D916 is admitted into evidence. The Prosecution has an opportunity, within the next 24 hours, to revisit the matters as far as completeness of the translation is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D60-0020.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, this is the 17 October 1995 Official Note of the interview with Boris Vunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, it's not an Official Note. It says it's a record on taking a statement, and it is actually signed by Mr. Vunic at the bottom. Mr. Vunic, on the 17th of October, Mr. Boris Vunic said, at the very top, that he was in Kistanje during the liberation. "I was going around houses for the purposes of finding war booty. When we came to the police station in Kistanje, right at the entrance, I found a 7.9-millimetre calibre M53 machine-gun which I immediately took for the purpose of keeping it for myself. After going through the other rooms in the above-mentioned, I found a military bag in a closet containing the following." I won't read it, but there is a description of all the different types of weaponry he found. He goes on to talk about in the middle of August going back into the liberated area with his brother Goran and taking tractors, taking them back to his home. He says, from the 1st of September to 14th September, he was in the field in Drvar. While in the field in Drvar, he found more weaponry and kept it for himself. Then he says: "At the end of September, not remembering the date, I went to the liberated areas again by tractor to the settlement Djevrska; and from one family house also owned by people I don't know, I took around ten new windows, put the same on the tractor, drove them home to Ladjevci." Now, Mr. Zganjer, this is on the 17th of October. You've seen that the Sibenik police had a work plan with Boris Vunic's name on it. In his statement to the police, Boris Vunic tells the police that he has all sorts of weaponry that he acquired and took home for his own personal use. What would you, as the prosecutor, expect to be the next step in the investigation with respect to Boris Vunic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement that was taken by the Sibenik police on the 17th of October, 1995, from Boris Vunic indicates that he, in fact, took for himself various weapons that he found in Djevrska, Ladjevci. At the time, well, I could tell what you I would have done, but this case was not in my jurisdiction at the time. But be that as it may, the statement itself dictates that the weapons be seized from Boris Vunic, that a search be carried out of his apartment, and that the weapons be taken away from him. It is possible that Boris Vunic might have agreed to hand over the weapons, making the search unnecessary. The weapons seized in this manner would then perhaps be examined by a ballistics expert. As far as the taking of tractors and other items is concerned, now it's a matter of judgement, whether to prosecute Boris Vunic for theft or some other offence. So that -- those would the actions that would stem from this statement that he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to P1063, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would you allow me to put one clarifying question. You said the theft, whether to prosecute Vunic for theft, that would be a matter of judgement. What did you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, a search would have to be carried out, and it -- we would have to ascertain whether Boris Vunic had, in fact, taken the tractor, as he claims here. The tractor should have been seized with appropriate receipt being issued to him, the weapons should have been seized from him, and then a criminal report should he been filed against him for theft or for unauthorised possession of a fire-arm. This is what his statement dictated quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it your experience that if such information reached the police in 1995 just after Operation Storm, that the appropriate action as you explained to us that should have been taken was actually taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at this point in time, I don't know that. I don't know whether any criminal reports were filed against Goran Vunic on the account of this statement, and whether he was prosecuted for what he had told the police officers here in this statement. We're talking about 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I asked you is whether such information in 1995 would have reached the police, whether, in fact, action as you described that would be appropriate to take on the basis of such information was taken in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, action would have been taken, should have been taken, because we face similar situations, countless of them; and many people were prosecuted for acts of this nature. I'm talking about theft, taking of various items such as tractors and so on from abandoned houses in the liberated territory. There were many such cases at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, especially since there were many of them, whether the capacity allowed for investigating them and prosecuting them, or whether there was just a certain percentage that would be investigated and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of the lack of personnel that we faced at that time, all the cases that came before the state attorney's office were dealt with. Actions were taken. So, in spite of the small number of personnel in the state attorney's office, we tried to deal with all those cases in a proper manner and to forward them to courts when there was enough evidence to prosecute persons against whom criminal reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking this question in relation to the answer when you said in relation to the tractors, for example, it was a matter of judgement. You didn't say, in relation to the weapons, that it was a matter of judgement whether or not to prosecute those cases; however, you did so in relation to the tractors.
