But you explained, then, that you had to establish whether he actually had stolen those tractors. Well, wouldn't be the same be true for establishing whether he had taken the weapons? I mean, you make a distinction there between the approach you would take in relation to the weapons and to the tractors. In the one, you say, "We'd go there, we'd search, we'd try to find them, they may have been given to the police already"; and in relation to the tractors, you said it required judgement, and when asked to explain you said, "Well, of course, you would have to establish the facts, and that would be true for the theft of weapons as well." So, therefore, I'm puzzled by the distinction you made there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your intervention is quite subtle and apposite. Let me be quite specific. There is no substantial difference between tractors and weapons. They are treated in the same manner; the procedure is same. This has to be reported and perpetrators have to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you very directly: Would it be that, in view of the type of stolen goods - weapons, which create a certain danger to society and tractors, which are primarily prejudicial to the owners of the tractors - that, in fact, priority was given to matters like weapons rather than to tractors and windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, priority had to be given to weapons, rather than to old beds, frames, window frames, or ancient washing machines and tractors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it, therefore, mean that theft of such goods as you mentioned were less vigorously investigated and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you're talk being weapons now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or the other goods being less vigorously investigated and prosecuted, which, of course, means that, I would say, the dangerous stuff - weaponry, ammunition, machine-guns - to be more vigorously investigated and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak about my experience while I worked in Sibenik and the time-period after the military and police Operation Storm. I think that my memory serves me right if I say that, in fact, we did have more people who were prosecuted for stealing furniture and furnishings than of people who took weapons. So, in the huge mass of criminal cases, many more dealt with household appliances than with weapons, cases where people found and then took the weapons. I'm talking about the Sibenik area, within the jurisdiction of the state attorney's office in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One follow-up question in that respect: Are you talking about absolute numbers, or are you talking about percentages? To clarify my question, if you investigate and prosecute ten cases of thefts of weapons, and if you investigate and prosecute ten cases of theft of tractors and windows, then the ten for the weapons might be 50 per cent if 20 of such cases were known; whereas, the tractors and the windows might be one per cent if a thousand cases were known. So, if you say more cases were prosecuted in relation to these less dangerous goods, that does not yet give an insight on the priority given and on the level of vigour with which investigations and prosecutions took place? So, to keep it simple: Were these, I would say, these less dangerous goods, were they from a point of view of percentage of investigations and prosecutions equally or less vigorously investigated and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say this once again. The cases involving theft of less dangerous goods were in the majority. There were far more of them. Let me precede this by saying that it was easier to identify the perpetrator of a theft that involved less dangerous goods, such as household appliances. Why? Because there were many cases of people going to the liberated area and loading beds, wardrobes, washing machines on to the tractors, and driving down the road, where they would be stopped and military and civilian police. Those items were then seized from those people and they were given appropriate receipts, and criminal reports were filed against them. Those people who took weapons did not go around recklessly and boldly with ten rifles hanging about their necks allowing themselves to be caught by the police. Those who stole weapons knew that this was a more delicate matter that had to be concealed in some manner, and this is why it was more difficult to identify those who stole or took weapons. This may be one of the reasons why the majority of criminal reports had to do with the theft of less dangerous goods, as opposed to the smaller number of cases that involved the theft of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's also the reason why I included in one of my previous questions limited the cases to those that had became known to the police. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm reminded that I forgot to ask that 1D60-0020, which is the statement of Boris Vunic, be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D917.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D917 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zganjer, you've told us that you expected, based on Mr. Boris Vunic's statement, that for the weapons, there would be an investigation or a search for those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could now take you back to P1063, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the letter of the state prosecutor in Zadar of the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we scroll down on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, it is concerning the Gosici and Varivode case and some of the names that were in the MUP action plan from the 15th, which I showed you a few minutes ago. I will tell on this list, if you go to at point 4, it's Ivica Petric and Nikola Rasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Number 5 is Nedeljko Mijic who also in the action plan and who also had already been interviewed by that point. Then if you look below paragraph -- the paragraph below paragraph number 5, the state prosecutor says, in relation to the stated: "Informative interviews should be conducted with the above-mentioned persons regarding the committing of the stated criminal offences, as well as with the eye-witnesses, and necessary verifications should be made concerning the possession of certain weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we go back to page 1 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday that it was, indeed, unusual that in a letter from the state prosecutor's office, in point 1, the name Vunic and then the first name is deleted, and by hand somebody wrote in Vunic, Goran. I believe yesterday you said you don't know when that insertion of the name took place. But my first question is : Again, you were the prosecutor in the Varivode and Gosici case. Did you find any evidence in the file before the date of this letter in which Goran Vunic had been considered a suspect by anyone in this case, in the case of Varivode, Gosici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could ask you, Counsel Misetic, to rephrase the question and be a bit more specific or precise. I have to say that I did not really understand it, and I would like to be able to you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is -- you have made statements in your statement about Goran Vunic being a suspect in the Varivode, Gosici case. My question to you is: Do you know of any evidence in the file, prior to this letter, which would indicate that Goran Vunic was a person of interest to any authority in the Republic of Croatia? When I say that -- when I say "a person of interest," I mean specifically in the Varivode, Gosici case.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I will be able to give you a specific answer. I don't know how I could know about some things about Goran Vunic before this letter was even drafted. If this letter or this motion by the county state attorney's office drafted on the 23rd of October, 1995, sent to the chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration by the Zadar state attorney's office, and if all this happened in 1995, at that time I covered an entirely different area, and I was not aware of this case. My knowledge about Goran Vunic, as a potential perpetrator of the crime in Gosici and Varivode, dates back to the time when I started taking action in order to try to identify the perpetrators of the crimes in Gosici and Varivode, if they were not the people who were charged with this -- with these crimes. So, after a decision was made not to prosecute people who were charged with those crimes, I start taking action to identify the actual, the real perpetrators. It is it only then that Goran Vunic became a suspect, as a potential perpetrator. This is when I learned from the memo sent by the military police that you showed me, the date is the 27th of June, 2002, what actually happened in relation to Goran Vunic and police activities. I learned about the alleged efforts to obstruct the investigation by the commander of the military police company, Nenad Mrkota, who obstructed the investigation that was put and trained by -- in a very proper manner by military police officer Damir Simic. The question then is why Nenad Mrkota did this in relation to Goran Vunic. Why is it that, in 2005, he stepped in and prevented the search of the apartment and other premises used by Vunic, and why the weapons used -- the side arms and the other weapons used by the reconnaissance company were not seized. It is only then that Goran Vunic became, in my eyes, a potential suspect as one of the possible perpetrators of this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will take you through, now, why perhaps Mr. Mrkota stopped the investigation, if he did, at all. Let me ask you this question: In the state attorney's office, when you sent out a letter to someone else and put the official seal on the letter, in the copy that was retained for the file in the state attorney's office, it's true, is it not, that you wouldn't necessarily put a seal on the file copy? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not necessary, if we're talking about a copy that remained in the files, in the archives of the state attorney's office. But letters or documents that were sent to specific addressees, they had to have the stamp affixed, the case number, and a signature had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this document in its form in the file of the county state attorney's office in Zadar, which is 1D60-0024, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The file copy in the state attorney's office in Zadar has only Boro Vunic at point 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the -- the reference to the file copy. Now, we do not know whether it is a file copy. The Defence tenders this document. We do not know from where the Defence has got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, anticipating that precise objection, I contacted the chief prosecutor in Croatia, Mr. Bajic. While I was on my feet, he has sent a letter of confirmation that this is the file copy that they have in Zadar. We will disclose it to Ms. Mahindaratne. Should she have any other questions, she can address me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it that, during the next break, you and Ms. Mahindaratne will set together, to see whether there remains any dispute as to the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary we will translate the entire correspondence with Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zganjer, as you heard, Mr. Bajic has confirmed for us this morning that this is the file copy of the letter in Zadar. Who -- let me put it a different way? You have no idea who blocked out Boro, called Babac, in the original, and then hand wrote in Goran Vunic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this further now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked. I don't know if Ms. Mahindaratne wishes to MFI it until she looks at Mr. Bajic's correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will object to the document, Mr. President, because I wish the Chamber to examine both documents. In fact, I have, if the Chamber requires, I have brought printout hard copies of both documents, the Prosecution version and what the Defence has just tendered. You can see certain aspects on the Prosecution document which indicates as to what the original document is. For example, if you compare the signatures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you want to us look at both documents at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it should be marked for identification anyhow; and then perhaps after your discussions during the break, it will be clear to the Chamber where exactly what the problem is. And even if it would be true, what you say, that could be relevant information for this claim to consider; and that for that reason, whether it's a forgery or whatever the background may be, that it would be good to have it in evidence, just to consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Defence has objected to the Prosecution version. In fact, it is in the MFI state. So perhaps, you know, both documents can be tendered into evidence, and then the Trial Chamber will have the benefit of comparing both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour, as long as -- I have no objection to that. And in addition to that, if there is an issue still that Ms. Mahindaratne has that what I have put on the screen is confirmed by the state prosector in Croatia as filed [indiscernible] to me, then I will ask that the letter from Mr. Bajic to the Defence also be tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest -- first of all, we our at this moment hearing you, Mr. Misetic, and I have not asked over Defence counsel on the matter. I suggest that you sit together to see what joint conclusions you can draw; and then, on the basis of that, inform the Chamber. If there is any matter of admission into evidence remaining after that, of course, the Chamber will give its ruling on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it marked for identification for the time being, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D918, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, let's look at -- I'm not what sure what the P number is now. Just a moment. Yes. This is, I believe, being submitted by the bar table by the Prosecution, so I don't think it has a P number yet. It is 65 ter 6092 -- actually, I'm advised now it is P1072.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is Mr. Simic's operative plan of the 25th of October. In it, in the first paragraph, he references the county prosecutor office in Zadar letter as the basis for putting the work plan together that we've just looked at. And if we look at point 1 of the plan - and this letter is dated 25 October - point 1 of the plan says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in the English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Ascertain until 0800 hours, on 25 October 1995, the proper addresses of the following persons," and then he identifies Goran Vunic as one of the individuals. The letter is date -- or the plan is dated 25 October, and the plan requires that the address be obtained by 0800 hours. So, presumably, Mr. Simic is -- wrote this plan before 0800 hours on the 25th of October. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to the first page and scroll to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I ask you to look at the UR number. The UR number of the work plan in which Mr. Simic asks that the address of Goran Vunic be found by 0800 hours ends in 51. It's document 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if could I have 65 ter 6094, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the arrest warrants issued by Mr. Mr. Simic, again on the same day, 25 October. In point 1, he asked that Goran Vunic be addressed and he now has the address that he is seeking in the work plan. If you look up at the UR number, the arrest warrant document number is 45. Now, you, as a prosecutor, is there anything -- when you see that the work plan document number 51 and the arrest warrant is document 45, does that give you any suspicions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually don't know the way in which these reference numbers, file numbers, were written in these memos. The fact that in this particular file number the number 45 is mentioned, and in the previous one there is number 51, would indicate that this particular letter numbered 45 was written before the 51 one. However, if in document number 51 it is written that the address of Goran Vunic needs to be ascertained, this would mean that the address had already been ascertained by the time that letter was written, since we have this particular letter here stating the address. Those are my assumptions. However, the deadline given for ascertaining the address of Goran Vunic, i.e., 8.00, this is nothing out of the ordinary. That is the character of police work. This particular letter could have been written at 5.00 in the morning on the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's nothing particularly problematic to me with respect to the 0800 hours. What I wanted to point out was the difference between the UR numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go -- sorry. I am asked to clarify that 65 ter 6094 is, in fact, P1074, MFI. If we could go to P970 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is that Official Note of Damir Simic upon which Mr. Glavan relied in his 2002 letter to you. This Official Note has no class or UR number on it, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if in a criminal file, such as this, you've seen Mr. Simic on that very day enter documents into the file using the procedure of putting class and UR numbers on the file, on the documents that day - this document has no such identification on it - is it correct to say, Mr. Zganjer, that this document at any point in time between 25 October 1995 and 2002 could have been inserted into the file?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. This witness cannot answer that for -- in addition to which, Mr. Simic testified in this court, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss the evidence available to this ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that doesn't -- no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question, you objected to the question because you said the witness cannot answer that, and then you wanted to add something. So let's focus on whether the witness can answer it. Whether there is a possibility that it was inserted in the file, that possibility remains open if, first of all, if the witness would not know when it had been, so if we ask the witness whether he has any knowledge when it was inserted in the file and find out about his knowledge, then, of course, logic could assists us all well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am afraid I have to point out that the Prosecution has led evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to discuss evidence in the presence of the witness, at least if I do not know what it is, then I'm strongly opposing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, can I ask that the witness then be excused for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zganjer, could you please leave us for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, since the witness has left the courtroom, you will an opportunity also to now briefly discuss the evidence which is already before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, perhaps it's fair I stop Ms. Mahindaratne at a time when she wanted to do it in the presence of the witness, which I opposed, but now the witness is not there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Mr. Simic testified in this proceedings, and the Defence did not cross-examine Mr. Simic on this basis at all. In fact, he was cross-examined on a completely different basis. It was suggested to him that the investigation was prevented by Nenad Mrkota because Goran Vunic testified in the same case; that is, the status from suspect was converted to that of a witness. Now, there was never a suggestion made that the identities were wrong, that there was a Boris Vunic, or that the documents had been inserted. There was never a suggestion made to Mr. Simic that there was conspiracy involved or a fabrication of material. He would have been the only witness who could have answered these questions. Now the Defence is attempting to lead that evidence, if I may use the term with apologies, through the back door. This is it not the appropriate way to cross-examine witnesses. This witness in court cannot answer these questions. That is all I have to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't know whether he can answer the question, because he has not given an answer. We don't know what his knowledge exactly is. It could be, but it just imagining, that he heard from someone that he inserted a document in a file at a certain date. I don't know. I have to assume at this moment that you would not know either, Ms. Mahindaratne, but you have a clear suspicion that he might not know the answer to this question. Let's make it a very factual question. Mr. Misetic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now give the opportunity to Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is somewhat surprising to hear my esteemed colleague on the other side of the aisle now complain that I'm asking questions about Mr. Simic, given that she herself put on a series of documents of Mr. Simic's that she never put to Simic and that she left for Mr. Zganjer. I can go through them all for you. But now, suddenly, it is a problem when the Defence starts to cross-examine on the documents that she is trying to admit through this witness. The problem is she failed to put her case to Mr. Simic, failed to put these documents that Mr. Simic is the author of to Mr. Simic. May I suggest it that it is she who is trying to enter documents in through the back do you remember. I'm just trying to meet her case. Those are the simple facts. Now, with respect to why I'm putting these matters to this witness, not only is she trying to put the documents in through the back door, she, at paragraph 38, has Mr. Simic testifying that: "This investigation was prevented from being carried out by the commander of the military police company, Nenad Mrkota." Then: "I believe if this investigation had been carried out as planned, the real perpetrators of this crime may have been brought to trial. As far as I know, Goran Vunic was always mentioned in the capacity of the a suspect in relation to this case." Now, I'm entitled to challenge those assertions, particularly since Ms. Mahindaratne is putting those claims in through this witness. Moreover, Ms. Mahindaratne went so far, yesterday, as to claim that the conspiracy rises all the way to the commander of the 72nd MP Battalion, Mr. Budimir. Again, it's a matter that she never put to Mr. Simic, but she trying to get in through Mr. Zganjer. This is our response to her putting in Simic material through this witness, Your Honour. I might also add --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I might also add, with respect to the protected witness issue, I was putting to Mr. Simic matters that Prosecution witness Ive Kardum told the Trial Chamber that he had heard. So it is not without foundation that I put those matters to him, and I simply took what Mr. Kardum had said and put it to Mr. Simic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the exception of one document, all documents tendered through this witness were documents received by him, attached to the special report that was handed over to him by major Glavan. So I did not tender a single document of Mr. Simic with the exception of one document, which was a work plan which attached to the special report that was received by this witness. Now, I also want to point out that the Defence, both parties, have an obligation under Rule 90(H) to put to a witness the opposing suggestion, if the witness's testimony is contrary to the Defence or the Prosecution position. Now, Mr. Simic was here, and this position taken by the Defence was never put to him. He could have been the only person who could have answered whether he inserted a document or not. Now to bring this evidence after he has left court is unfair by the witness. That is all I have to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first ask before we continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I did put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I'm drawing your attention to page 62, line 7, where you're making reference to paragraph 38, and then you say Mr. Simic testified. May I take it that you wanted to refer to Mr. Zganjer in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been corrected now. Let me just take one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both parties blame each other for not having put questions to witnesses during the examination either in chief or cross-examination at a certain stage. The parties will forgive the Chamber for not having every detail available immediately and to see what merits there are in those positions. We have considered the matter. And if questions were not put to a witness, and if there's a position taken that this is unfair and that therefore questions should not be put to this witness, of course, there are two remedies to prohibit putting any further questions to this witness or to consider at a later stage whether the questions and answers given by this witness viewed in the totality of the evidence would urge the Chamber or would justify to call Mr. Simic again to answer questions you say he is the only one who could answer. The Chamber has considered the matter and will allow Mr. Misetic to proceed and will consider at any later stage whether questions and answers will create a need to re-call Mr. Simic. Could the witness be brought in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at the clock. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so can I complete the record, in terms when you look back at the transcript later, I believe I did put matters to Mr. Simic. I specifically asked him whether he advised anyone of what he wrote in this Official Note. He said with respect to -- the only person he said is with respect to Boro Milas, and he said: "I think I told him orally." I also specifically asked hem whether he addressed this note or sent this in writing to anyone else, and he said "No." So, to that extent, Your Honour, I did put it to him, and my suggestion simply was that this is a document that nobody else can vouch for expect Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if at any later stage the parties will make submissions on whether or not Mr. Simic whether there's a need to re-call Mr. Simic, then we'll get all these details you have already put on the record by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps it is it better that someone informs Mr. Zganjer that it's time for coffee anyhow, and that we'd like to see him back after the break. Mr. Misetic, could you give us an impression on how much more time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say a half an hour at the max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us an indication on as matters stand now how much time would you need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At the most, half an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So with half an hour and half an hour, that would take us to the end of today's session. Therefore, I, out of caution, inquire with Cermak Defence, still no questions. We will have a break and we will resume at twenty minutes to 1.00. The parties are urged to check their cross-examination and re-examination, to see, in fact, wether we can complete the examination of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, when we were discussing a procedural matter, we were so close to a break that we took a break by then. This is just as an explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, let me ask it a different way. The Official Note on the screen, you don't have any information as to when that note was put in the file, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this Official Note as an attachment to a document that was submitted to me on the 27th of June, 2002. This was part of the special report from the military police, the crime investigation division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It contained this Official Note, and this is the first time that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, let me ask you the following question, and it is somewhat hypothetical but relevant to this issue. If, in the Croatian system, a search warrant is issued for person A, but should have been issued for person B, and person A and B live together in the same house, pursuant to the search warrant misnamed under person A, the authorities find incriminating evidence against person B, assume for the sake of argument that the search warrant was defective, would the evidence obtained purpose to the defective search warrant cause any difficulties in the prosecution of person B, under the Croatian system?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrest warrant has to specify the person that is to be brought into custody. If the person who is brought into custody is not the person named in the arrest warrants, then we are entering the zone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was about a search warrant; that is, to search the premises to see whether any evidential material, any evidence can you found there, not about arresting a person. So the search warrant, saying there's a suspicion against Mr. A, we allow the search of the premises where he lives; A by the way is a mistake, because the suspicion is against B; and now during this search on this premises, incriminating evidence is found in relation B, whose name is not appearing on the search warrant. Would that cause problems later on in using that evidence in a case against B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Perhaps I'm unable to grasp this question due to my own failings. Can we perhaps have -- clarify this in this manner: We have warrant for the arrest of a certain person, that's one situation; and then we also have the search warrant for the search of certain premises. So Counsel Misetic I would like you to clarify and specify this, and I will be happy to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... permission, Mr. President, I will tell him in Croatian, because I'm not sure what translation is he receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Search warrant, not arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the arrest warrant lists person A, and it is erroneous because it actually pertains to person B, and they live in the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll check the transcript later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A search of a house is carried out based on the warrant that lists person A, and incriminating evidence against person B is found. Now, can this evidence be used against person B in criminal proceedings, or would there be problems because the evidence was found on the basis of an erroneous search warrant?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a search warrant pertains to the premises where person A is residing or is present, and if, in the course of the premises used by person A, items are found that do not belong to person A but to person B, I think that, in that case, it would be a valid search, and I think that evidence found in the premises used by person A could also be used as evidence in criminal proceedings in a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question was a bit more specific than that. So we're talking about a defective search warrant against person A. What I mean is that the search warrant should have been issued for person B, but due to a mistake, person A is listed in the search, is named in the search warrant. So there was no factual basis for the search of person A's house, but due to a mistake, the defective search warrant was issued. Could this engender any problems in future criminal proceedings against person B?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there could problems because the validity of evidence obtained in this manner could be questioned if the search warrant named person A instead of person B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Mr. Zganjer. You have some testimony here, and I understand very much that you're knowledge of what Mr. Mrkota may or may not have done in 1995 is based on what you were told by Mr. Glavan in 2002. I understand that. However, part of your statement, at paragraph 38, says that: "The investigation was prevented from being carried out by commander of the military police company, Nenad Mrkota." Then you go on to say: "I believe if this investigation had within carried out as planned, the real perpetrators of this crime may have been brought it trial." Now, my question to you is: As you were considering and as you consider this evidence, in your judgement, is it possible, in light of what I have shown you in terms of the state of the evidence against Goran Vunic prior to that letter of the 23rd of October, that Commander Mrkota stopped the search of the premises of Goran Vunic, on the basis that he himself had no information that Goran Vunic was the target of the investigation and thought that it could jeopardize the results of the search of the home of Boris Vunic, because the search warrant would have been issued in the wrong Vunic's name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I have to say, to be consistent with what I said before, when I spoke about Nenad Mrkota, I was talking about the special report from the military police administration, the CID. Now, whether the claims contained in the special report would be corroborated in the course of the proceedings, now, that's a whole different question. We talked about the validity of evidence given that the search warrant erroneously named such-and-such a person. I cannot rule out the possibility that this might have been the reason why Nenad Mrkota, if at all, if he did, in fact, prohibited any further actions and the search from going on. But what is quite clear to me is the fact that Nenad Mrkota, Commander Mrkota, if he was motivated by those reasons to prevent a search, should have explained that. He had to clarify whether this was Boris or Goran Vunic, and then we would know what to do, how to proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at that exact question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D60-0042 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from the 26th of January, 1996, Zadar-Knin crime police department. The subject is "Murders by unknown perpetrators, ballistics report." There are several dates about what the requests. The last two are 26 October and 22 November, 1995. Here, the crime police sector is reporting on forensic analysis on weapons seized from individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we can go in the English to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now -- I draw your attention to binder number 13. One of the ballistics tested done was on a Kalashnikov automatic rifle, calibre 7.62-millimetre, serial number, seized from Boris Vunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12 -- actually, page 11, please, of the English -- actually, page 10 then. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a letter from the 19th of May, 1997, again sending weapons which have been fired for the purpose of solving the murders by unknown perpetrators in the area of the Zadar-Knin police administration in the time-period between 28 September 1995 and 3 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At number 26, we have the weapon of Boris Vunic. Now, on the basis of these documents from 1996 and 1997, would it appear to you that at some point in time, the authorities, in fact, did get the weapons, or get at least one weapon, from Boris Vunic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only would that have appear to me, but the documents you're showing me indicate that the subject of ballistics examination included the weapons found on Boris Vunic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 1D60-0042 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D919.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar and Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D919 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zganjer, I also note that in the actual judgement in the Varivode case in 1997, it's a 114-page judgement which has been tendered by the Prosecution in its bar table submission. There is no reference whatsoever to Goran Vunic, but there are three references to Boris Vunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the English, it's at page 18, page 52, and page 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm sure you reviewed that judgement many times. If Goran Vunic had -- it had been alleged at any point that Goran Vunic was one of the persons in Varivode and/or Gosici at the time of these murders, based on your experience, would his name have come up during the trial in the Varivode case or in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In fact, we've been discussing Vunices all this time, Boris and Goran. I believe that these are, in fact, two brothers. As far as I'm able to remember now, Goran Vunic did have a brother. Whether his name was Boris or not, I don't know. I can't recall all the details of the judgement; and, consequently, I can't give you a specific answer to that question, unfortunately. I really can't tell you whether the names of Boris and Goran Vunic were mentioned in the judgement. What I do remember is the fact that the ballistics examination indicated that none of the weapons seized and which were subjected to ballistics examination included the rifle which would have matched the bullet casings found at the scene in Gosici and Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to switch topics, so I don't know if there are any additional questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One of the question I did have was, actually, is that one of the suspects in the MUP work plan from 15 October and mentioned throughout the rest of the Varivode case was a gentleman named Nedeljko Mijic. Are you familiar with that gentleman's name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the person by the name of Nedeljko Mijic was one of the persons in -- accused for the murder in Varivode or Gosici. At any rate, a person by the name of Nedeljko Mijic was one of the persons charged with this incident. I can't be sure whether it was in Gosici or in Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I ask you that question because of a different murder, or two murders, that took place in the area of Kakanj on or around the 18th August. You, in your statement, talk about the fact that you personally met with one of the victims who was not killed but was seriously injured in that that incident, Mr. Mirko Ognjenovic, who testified before this Trial Chamber. Mr. Ognjenovic, in his statements and before this Trial Chamber, said that one of the individuals who was in a uniform turned to the other individual and referred to him as Nedeljko. Now, I understand that there, in theory, could be many people with that first name. But in light of the fact that that murder and the Gosici murders took place roughly nine or ten days apart, in the course of your investigation of the Kakanj murders, did you investigate Nedeljko Mijic as a potential perpetrator of those murders.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a lot of time has elapsed. As far as I'm able to remember now, I think that, together with a police officer, I personally spoke to this person, Ognjenovic, in Kakanj. I think that Mr. Ognjenovic recounted the circumstances surrounding the death of these two individuals to me and the policeman with me. I believe he even showed us some photographs he had on him. The two persons killed were, in fact, exhumed subsequently in the cemetery in Zadar, if I'm not mistaken. I might be at risk of making a mistake, but as far as I remember, Mr. Ognjenovic was telling us at the time about the correspondence between the two either members of the Croatian army or merely two individuals wearing HV uniforms. I believe he told us at the time that one of the persons addressed the other one by Nedjo. That was everything Mr. Ognjenovic told us. I don't believe that he used the full name Nedjelko. I think that he told the name was or Nidjo or Nedjo. Well, now that person who was referred to as addressing the other one as Nedjo or Nidjo supposedly would have tried to dissuade the other person from doing what he was about to do, but I don't think he used the full name when telling us the story of Nedjelko. I think he used the name of Nedjo. I think it was the conversation taking place between the two, and one of them was called Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question on another matter. You were shown a letter from Mr. Separovic, which is Exhibit D912 now, this morning by Mr. Mikulicic, in which Mr. Separovic asks the military courts to send him their files so that those files can be sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. From a disciplinary perspective, who did military prosecutors answer to ultimately for their work?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor was directly subordinate to the hierarchy of the state attorney's offices. I, as a deputy of a military prosecutor, was directly answerable to the military prosecutor of my district in Split; whereas, my prosecutor for the district in Split - that was Mr. Simic - was directly responsible to the state attorney of Republic of Croatia, and that was the only line of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did the commander of the Split Military District - in this case, General Ante Gotovina - issue an order to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Absolutely not. I would answer such a question with a counterquestion: Could have the military prosecutor suggested or ordered to General Gotovina which axis he should use in an attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the same question concerning discipline with respect to military judges. Who did military judges answer to vertically?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were directly subordinate to the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia -- or rather, the county court and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia. Of course, you, Counsel Misetic, know that full well, that this is a different sort of subordination to that of military prosecutors. The Supreme Court cannot order a judge of a military court what sort of a judgement he should render; however, the national state attorney could have instructed a military prosecutor on how to proceed in a given case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And my final topic, Mr. Zganjer, Mr. Ive Kardum testified before this Trial Chamber that in his assessment between 1991 and 1995, approximately 10.000 homes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. Mr. Zganjer is a practice in this -- established in the -- in this Court as to how to put other witness's testimony to a witness in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if he ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we have not heard the question yet, but you are aware of this practice, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm ask being about, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Ive Kardum testified before this Trial Chamber that approximately 10.000 homes had been burned down between 1991 and 1995 of ethnic Croats in the occupied areas. My question to you is: Did you prosecute people after Operation Storm for the burning down of the homes of Croats during the occupation; and, if so, how many; and, if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few such cases in the area of the Sibenik county state attorney's office. Now, why didn't we process such crimes, or why didn't we receive any criminal reports for such offences? Well, you see, it was very difficult to ascertain who of the members of which army set which houses on fire. It is a fact that many homes of Croats were burnt. However, after the war, it was difficult to ascertain which of the members of the enemy army set fire to which house. It was difficult to ascertain, and there were only a handful of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zganjer, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that there may be an issue on the transcript. At page 68, line 2, it says "arrest warrant." Yes. I believe I was speaking in Croatian at the time, and I believe I said "search warrant" and not "arrest warrant" in line 2, page 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that the matter finally became clear on what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would urge the parties to see if you could finish well within a half-hour from now, because there are a few procedural matters I would like to deal with which are of an urgent character. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if you could bring up D919, please, on the screen; D919, the weapons and analysis document that Defence just tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will read it while the document comes up. Mr. Zganjer, in fact, you were shown this document. If you could go to the page 1D00 -- I don't think this is -- I will just read out the -- because Mr. Misetic himself indicated the period for which he said these weapons were obtained. "And it is for criminal proceedings for murders by unknown perpetrators in the area of Zadar-Knin police administration in the time-period between 28 September 1995 and 3 October 1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't know in which document that information is, but I don't think Mr. Misetic will dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, these weapons were obtained and analysed for crimes committed for that period, as I understand, from that document; that is, 28 September 1995 and 3 October 1995. Is that correct, Mr. Zganjer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you go perhaps to the page 1D60-0064. I think it must be about page 7 or 8 of the English version. Yes, we have that page, and then the corresponding page on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, isn't it, Mr. Zganjer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could bring up on the screen, Mr. Registrar, P970. If you could take -- yes. If you could take the page down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you note that that paragraph numbered 1, it records that Goran Vunic, and his details are given, member of the 113th Infantry Brigade, is wanted for committing a crime on an undetermined day in August 1995, together with two others as yet unidentified men, and the killing incident is with regard to a person named Gojko Lezajic. So, based on the date of offence, can you -- is it correct that the weapons analysis document, which had crimes indicated for the period 28 September 1995 to 3rd October 1995, does not cover this particular crime for which Mr. Goran Vunic is wanted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The time-period mentioned in the previous document does not correspond to the period mentioned in this Official Note, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... be allowed to complete the answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could please ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Zganjer, if you have anything else to say.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I may observe, the dates mentioned in these submissions and in the evidence in this case is not as important. When you seize certain weaponry, you cannot be sure that there are reasons to suspect that the weapons were used between a certain period, June and September. It will be only through ballistics examination once it's done that you may realize that there was a crime committed even before that date. This is something that is simply possible. Once you've seized a concern amount of weapons, you can't say, "Yes, we do have reasons to suspect that the weapons may have been used to commit crimes between 1st September and 30 October." The ballistics examination will examine the casings found at a crime scene even -- that were there even before the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, of course, it can always be possible that from that weapon --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have D914, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I was given only a very few minutes, and I will be grateful if you could respond to my questions briefly, because we're running out of the time. I just want you to take note of a document that I'm about to show you. This was just tendered by the Defence. If could you go to page -- the third page, do you note, at the top of page, the investigating officer who arrested Mr. Boris Vunic is recorded as "F. Mikulandra"? If could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for foundation that he arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, because it is it noted there, and then according to D917, Mr. Mikulandra has recorded his interview. These are Defence documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he was arrested, but that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's on the record then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then can we have D917, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is it the record of interview with Boris Vunic, and at the interview, Mr. Mikulandra present, according to the first page of the document. If you see, according to this first page, it mentions that he is being investigated: "In the course of proceeding, pursuant Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, for reasonable suspicion of committing a criminal offence of aggravated theft as described in Article 126," and the rest of the Criminal Code details are given. Now, so, there is no record that he has been brought in for a case of -- on suspicion of a killing incident in Gosici here, is there, Mr. Zganjer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As far as I'm able to recall his statement, he does not speak of any possible knowledge he may have of the events in Varivode and Gosici, and I'm referring to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If he could go, Mr. Registrar, right down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It records that: "At the beginning of Operation Storm, to be more exact on 4 August 1995, I was in the Croatian army 15th Home Guard Regiment in the composition of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion." Your testimony was, and we have tendered a number of documents, where Goran Vunic was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Boris Vunic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I know. I am referring to Goran Vunic. Your testimony was that Goran Vunic was a platoon commander of the 113th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then if we could have P10 -- I'm sorry, P1072.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that is the work plan of the -- the Sibenik military police company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 on English version, and, Mr. Registrar, if I could just go down on the B/C/S -- sorry, the Croatian version. Yeah. No, I'm sorry. It's also page 2 of the Croatian version, and right at the bottom of the page on both versions, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note that one of the officers who is sent to search the premises of Goran Vunic is Frane Mikulandra? He is assisting the military police in this search activity. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. Whether he is assisting or not, his name on the page. What happened, whether he even knew his name was on the page, there is no foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please respond to this question, Mr. Zganjer: Was the Sibenik criminal military police conducting this particular investigation in cooperation with the Sibenik military police administration officers -- I'm sorry, Sibenik civilian police officers who belonged to the Sibenik police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this work plan - and I don't know whether it was really implemented or not - indicates that this was a coordinated activity, which was part of the criminal investigation. It was carried out in a coordinated manner both by the military police and the general duty police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have just one last document, Mr. Registrar, P1074.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while that is coming up, Mr. Zganjer, that is the special report that was sent to you -- I'm sorry, that is the investigation plan of the criminal military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry I asked for the wrong document. I beg your pardon, Mr. Registrar. If could I have P1073.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked questions about the search warrant as to whether, if there were search defects in a search warrant, what the impact would be. You were also asked the question as to whether is it possible that Mr. Mrkota may have prevented the investigation from being carried forward because he felt there was no evidence against Goran Vunic. Now, I'd like to draw your attention, while this document is on the screen, to your supplementary statement, and I don't know whether you have it with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you could just --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you look at paragraph 41, you -- you're referring to the search warrant. And for lack of time I will go to the particular line, which is about the seventh line, where you say: "If for any reason the warrant cannot executed, then the authority which is required to execute the warrant - in this case, the Sibenik criminal military police - have to report such fact to court. I believe the military prosecutor in Split to whom this search warrant was also delivered should have inquired as to the execution." Now, are aware of any report whatsoever or any documents existing in these criminal files where Mr. Nenad Mrkota or anyone from the Sibenik criminal military police reporting to the investigating judge as to why the warrant was not executed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the military police company commander, Mr. Nenad Mrkota, military police in Sibenik, told the military prosecutor and the investigating judge why this search warrant was not executed. The search warrant is quite clear and precise, and it pertains to the search of the premises in Sibenik at number 6 Zagrebacka Street, and a room in the Monting [phoen] Hotel, occupant which is Goran Vunic, son of Ante. So I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is going too deep. The question was limited to whether you were aware of any reasons being reported, not on whether it was difficult to execute the search warrant. I understood your answer to be that you don't know of any such reasons being reported. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, you did also -- I want to bring to your notice that the address of the place to be searched is indicated in the search warrant. Thank you, Mr. Zganjer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just have one more -- Mr. President I if could just have a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That minute is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could quickly have document P1007.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While that document is it being brought up, Mr. Zganjer, you were asked questions by Mr. Mikulicic about the military discipline records. I know you have been a military prosecutor, but since it has been some time, it is possible that you may have forgotten. I want to show you a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go to page 2 of the Croatian version and page 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you stated that where a person was prosecuted in a military court, there would not be a parallel proceeding against that same person, same member of the military in the disciplinary courts. Now, do you note Article number 8, where it is stated, I believe, from paragraph 3: "The military disciplinary court finds that the offence against military discipline is, in fact, a minor one, shall issue a disciplinary measure. "If a criminal offence is found to be a major violation of military discipline, the offender my also answer before ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... may also answer before a military disciplinary court if this is in the particular interest of the armed service. "Proceedings before military disciplinary courts shall be conducted independently of the proceedings or outcome of the criminal case." Do you note from that, Mr. Zganjer, that what you said, or your answer to Mr. Mikulicic's question, was incorrect. That, in fact, where a crime is prosecuted in a military court, there can be a parallel disciplinary proceedings in the military disciplinary courts -- military disciplinary tribunals?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, I was not specific enough. These are the rules of service from 1992, but I cannot claim this. I really don't know whether and in how many cases the special interests of the service resulted in parallel military disciplinary proceedings against persons who were, at the time, criminally prosecuted. I really don't know. If there were such cases, and if there were, how many of them, cases where the same person would face for the same acts, for the same offences, both the military disciplinary proceedings parallel with the criminal proceedings for reasons that had to do with special interest of the service. I simply cannot envisage a situation where person A, an active duty serviceman, is being tried before a military court for murder, and that a military disciplinary proceedings are conducted before the military disciplinary tribunal for the same offence. But I have to say this with a caveat, I'm not sure whether I'm correct, but I'm not sure whether in 1992, when the rules of service were adopted, whether military disciplinary prosecutor's offices were in place and military disciplinary tribunals were in place, or whether they were, in fact, established at a later date. So take this with a grain of salt, I allow for the possibility that I may not be right. But as far as I can recall, the prosecutor's office and tribunals for military disciplinary matters were established only in 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zganjer, for responding to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zganjer, I have one question, if could you perhaps briefly answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that an Official Note containing an interview, or at least reflecting what was said during an interview with a suspected person, should be removed from the case file. Do I understand that the same does not apply, even though not being evidence, but that the same does not apply in relation to Official Notes reflecting what a witness would have told the police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO ZGANJER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Official Notes about interviews with suspects are removed from the case file, as are Official Notes on interviews conducted with citizens who provide information about a crime. Both kinds of notes are removed from the file and cannot be used as evidence at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Have the questions by the Bench or questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions? Then, Mr. Zganjer, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for come ago long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that you were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One matter which is relatively urgent. I would like to deal with it briefly; that is, I would like to deliver a decision. It is a decision on the Gotovina Defence's Rule 92 bis motion. On the 4th of November, 2008, the Gotovina Defence filed a motion for admission of a statement pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The statement in question was given by a person to the Prosecution in 1999, and subsequently disclosed to the Defence. That person is not on the Prosecution's witness list. On the 6th of November, 2008, the Cermak and Markac Defence informed the Chamber that they do not oppose the motion. These submissions can be find at transcript pages 11.214. On the 10th of November, 2008, the Prosecution filed its response, opposing the motion. The Prosecution argued that the Gotovina Defence had not shown why it should be allowed to call a witness during the Prosecution case. The Prosecution added that, should the Chamber decide to allow the Gotovina Defence to do so, the person in question should be called for cross-examination. Rule 85 sets out the sequence of presentation of evidence during trial, with the presentation of the evidence for the Prosecution preceding that of the Defence. Presentation of evidence includes introducing testimony of witnesses viva voce, as well as pursuant to Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, 92 quater. The Chamber may, if it is in the interests of justice, decide to vary the sequence of presentation of evidence set out in Rule 85. The Gotovina Defence has not provided any reasons why it would be in the interests of justice to introduce the testimony of the person in question now, during the Prosecution's case, as opposed to during a possible Defence case. If the Gotovina Defence intends to use the statement during cross-examination of witnesses called by the Prosecution, it may do so without having the statement admitted into evidence. This may be done by simply reading the relevant portions of the statement to the Prosecution witness and then seeking his or her comments. This does not mean that the relevant portions enter into evidence. The Chamber does not find that it is in the interests of justice to allow the Gotovina Defence to introduce the evidence of the person in question during the Prosecution's presentation of evidence. The Chamber, therefore, denies the motion, without prejudice, to any further motion by the Defence, with regard to the admission of the statement. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Very briefly, I see Mr. Hedaraly arrived. He would be here during the last session of the today. He must have noticed that we did not have sufficient time to discuss the photo spread issue in relation to Witness 3, but the Chamber is aware of the need to further deal with the matter and we'll find a moment for that very soon. Then, there is another matter in which there was an issue about objections against admission into evidence of P703, which is still marked for identification. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to see whether P703 is still needed to be tendered, since P177 is virtually the same document, although under a different ERN number, and was admitted into evidence on the 1st of May, 2008. Similarly, Defence is invited to explain why objections were raised now, the issue being that Mr. Marti could not be questioned on the matter, where this document had been in evidence already since the 1st of May, whether the objection stands. Finally, the Chamber received information that for the next witness, I think it was the Gotovina Defence that indicated that it would need ten hours. As always, the Chamber will closely follow the course of how the cross-examination goes. The Chamber hopes, at the same time, that where, now and then, we have urged the parties to take less time, that this does not result in asking for more time in the beginning, so as to end at the very end with the same amount one has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I am not entering any debate on the matter, but just to let you know, the Chamber will, as always, follow how the time in cross-examination is spent to see whether, finally, it would allow to you spend the ten hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, Your Honour, that that goes without saying. Every time we're on our feet, we are aware that you are following how we are using our time. Let me just state that the reason is that I, at this point, do intend to take the ten hours, and it directly relates to the fact that the Prosecution has decided not to call certain witnesses in its case in chief which were on their witness list concerning many relevant issue before the Trial Chamber. We will attempt to cover them all with this witness, and, perhaps, we wouldn't have the need for extra witnesses that the Prosecution now does not intend to call. So there is really a valid reason why we need that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say that a major portion of the time spent may be spent under Rule 90(H), which says that if you go beyond what is asked through witness in chief, if the witness who is available --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, the witness does refer to all relevant issues in his statement, and he has personal knowledge of the issues. Some witnesses would have perhaps been more knowledgeable, but I will certainly put those matters to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll closely follow the course you take. We'll adjourn for the day, and, again, apologies for the six stolen minutes. We will resume tomorrow, Thursday, 13th of November, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
